We introduce a novel, detector-free matching approach that leverages a
Transformer-based model to identify correspondences between pixels in two images.
By relying on keypoints detected by an existing model, our method efficiently
establishes dense correspondences across the entire image in under 100 milliseconds,
achieving a rate of 20-30 times faster than traditional point-to-point matching
methods. This enables our approach to be utilized in high-speed video applications,
such as real-time video editing and 3D reconstruction. We evaluate our method's
performance using a range of metrics and demonstrate its effectiveness on several
benchmarks, including 2D and 3D tasks.

The use of Stokes inversion to derive solar magnetic field maps has become a standard practice, with the goal of creating a comprehensive, three-dimensional magnetic field model. However, the process of extracting vector magnetic field data from observations is complex and prone to errors, particularly when it comes to determining the sign of polarity. As a result, the accuracy of inferred vector magnetic field data is often compromised by these limitations. To address these issues, we employed machine learning techniques to identify and mitigate bias in solar vector magnetic field data derived from the Solar Dynamics Observatory's HiFI inversion dataset. By removing the bias, we found that the precision of the vector magnetic field data improved significantly, with lower values of precision error for the magnetic field strength, direction, and polarity.

This study presents a novel demand side management strategy that leverages an aggregative game framework. The approach involves dividing consumers into a group and implementing a uniform instantaneous load pricing policy. To minimize energy consumption, consumers adjust their appliance usage according to a scheduled plan. The proposed scheme ensures that users adhere to the planned schedule and achieve a cost-minimizing outcome. The effectiveness of this strategy is demonstrated through simulation using real-world data, which shows that it can reduce peak demand and achieve a cost-minimizing outcome.

In a modified theory of gravity known as Rastall theory, researchers investigated how gravity affects Hawking radiation from charged black strings. They discovered that, unlike in Einstein's theory of general relativity, these black strings have non-zero Ricci scalar curvature and a non-zero cosmological constant. By solving the Einstein-like equations for these black strings, they found that the metric tensor components and associated physical quantities such as temperature and entropy exhibit complex behavior influenced by the charge and cosmological constant. Furthermore, when Hawking radiation occurs, it leads to a decrease in the black string's mass and area, causing the string to shrink and eventually disappear. However, the radiation's effect on the string's rotation velocity is dependent on the cosmological constant, and the string may either continue to shrink with or without rotation, depending on the value of the cosmological constant.

The behavior of sequences of function values at rational points in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem is examined in relation to the spectral radius of corresponding unitary operators. It is demonstrated that this spectral radius serves as a bound on the asymptotic convergence rates for a broad class of ergodic averages, encompassing those associated with actions of commutative semigroups. Moreover, it is found that this spectral radius is the optimal limit that can be attained by sequences of ergodic averages. The results are applicable to any compact topological group G when considering weakly mixing actions, and specifically, when G is a compact Lie group, they are shown to be expressible in terms of invariant Haar measures.

We introduce a method that uses the Gaia satellite's photometric and spectroscopic data to automatically identify metal-poor stars. The technique involves analyzing the H$\alpha$ absorption line in stellar spectra to determine its equivalent width, and then applying a machine learning model based on support vector classification. This model, trained on synthetic spectra generated by the MOOG linelist, is capable of accurately identifying metal-poor stars with high precision. We tested the technique on a sample of 10,000 synthetic spectra with varying levels of metallicity and found that it achieved an accuracy of 95% for stars with [Fe/H] values below -2.0 and an accuracy of 85% for stars with [Fe/H] values below -3.0.

Wildfires pose significant threats to people, property, and ecosystems worldwide.
The increasing frequency and severity of these blazes pose substantial risks
to human safety, infrastructure, and the environment. To better understand and
mitigate wildfire impacts, it is crucial to analyze and forecast seasonal fire
activity. This involves examining historical data to identify patterns in fire
occurrence and severity, and developing predictive models to forecast future
activity. This research aims to develop a framework for assessing and
forecasting seasonal wildfire activity using satellite-derived burned area
data. This framework can be applied globally, and is demonstrated here using data
from Australia and the United States.

This study examines the relationship between different methods of evaluating word complexity in a large corpus of English words, and investigates how these methods correlate with various measures of a word's morphological structure. By analyzing a dataset of 100,000 words, the study finds a strong connection between one of the complexity measures and a range of other factors, including the frequency of a word's individual morphemes and the frequency of their combinations. The results also suggest that words with high morphological complexity tend to have more varied and less common grammatical functions.

The presence of small-scale gravitational lensing in galaxy clusters can provide valuable insights into the behavior of dark matter. By analyzing the distortions in background galaxy shapes, researchers can map out dark matter's subhalo distribution. This study compares self-interacting dark matter models with a standard cold dark matter scenario, using data from the Gravlens catalog. By examining the relationship between tangential distortion profiles and halo mass, the researchers found that a non-interacting CDM model fails to match the data, while a SI dark matter model with a moderate interaction cross-section of $10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2\,\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ fits the observations well. This cross-section is consistent with previous findings from strong lensing data, and the results are robust against variations in halo mass definition and tangential distortion profiles.

This study focuses on simplifying dynamic models that utilize multiple variables, despite only having access to a limited number of observable parameters. The objective is to identify the most basic model that can accurately process the available data and effectively predict results, using a maximum likelihood estimation approach. To achieve this, an information-theoretic framework is developed to determine the most concise model that fits the given data, based on the principle of minimum description length. A practical algorithm is also introduced to streamline models, incorporating model structure and parameter uncertainty. The proposed method is then evaluated using simulated data from a Lotka-Volterra model, and further applications are explored in the fields of network medicine and autonomous driving.

A novel approach to Automated Feature Extraction using Fast-ACF has been developed. Fast-ACF is an efficient variant of Automated Feature Extraction that generates feature engineering rules with lower memory usage and faster computation times compared to its predecessor. The newly introduced M-ar-K-Fast variant builds upon Fast-ACF by incorporating multi-relational reasoning capabilities. As a result, M-ar-K-Fast is capable of producing more complex feature engineering rules that can combine multiple attributes, thereby expanding its applicability to domains with limited attribute connectivity. Experimental results demonstrate that M-ar-K-Fast is a reliable and scalable solution that can effectively handle large datasets with multiple attributes.

Detecting incidents on social media in real-time is a crucial task that can aid emergency response and management. Current methods utilizing social media feeds are limited by their dependence on specific keywords, which often fail to identify incidents like building fires or traffic accidents. To overcome this, we've developed a new approach that leverages geotagged social media posts to identify incidents as they unfold. By combining spatial and temporal features from posts, our method can pinpoint anomalies and distinguish actual incidents from random events. To test the effectiveness of our approach, we've conducted a study using over 1.5 million Twitter posts related to 150 incidents across 5 countries, demonstrating its ability to accurately identify incidents in real-time.

This research focuses on resolving a growth optimal issue related to measure elliptic equations, which involves determining the maximum possible growth rate of the nonlinearity in a given equation while maintaining solvability for all radially symmetric harmonic potentials within a specified Sobolev space. We also investigate similar problems for vector-valued equations and provide additional results on the solvability of these equations.

Using computational tools, researchers explored the yttrium-cobalt-boron phase space to discover new materials with high cobalt content. They utilized the Generalized Finitely Ranged Clustering Genetic algorithm to identify 13 new cobalt-abundant compounds, which were found to have higher cobalt content than the well-known Co$_{15}$B$_{2}$ phase. These newly discovered compounds were predicted to have improved thermoelectric properties compared to existing ones.

In display advertising, the goal of risk-aware ad bidding is to maximize revenue while limiting loss due to bid restrictions and unmet demand. However, existing approaches either adapt to market conditions or account for risk, but not both. This paper addresses this gap by developing a dynamic bidding strategy that adjusts its risk level in response to market conditions and demand. The proposed method involves an online algorithm that allocates budget to impressions, and a post-processing step that reoptimizes the budget allocation to meet a target risk level. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves better revenue and reduced loss compared to both adaptive and risk-aware methods.

We investigate the relationship between quantum correlations in guidance and Wigner negativity in continuous-variable quantum information, focusing on the underlying physical principles. First, we demonstrate that Wigner negativity is a reliable indicator of quantum entanglement in terms of the quantum Fisher information, which measures quantum correlations in guidance. Additionally, we establish that both the quantum Fisher information and average path-length-based guidance quantum correlations are necessary conditions for Wigner negativity. Furthermore, we explore the connection between Wigner negativity and the quantum Fisher information in terms of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, revealing that the Heisenberg uncertainty principle alone is insufficient to guarantee Wigner negativity.

This study examines the security properties of a quantum key distribution (QKD) system that employs non-uniform random seeds within the privacy amplification process. To evaluate the impact of these seeds, we developed a probability model that accounts for their varying entropy levels. Our analysis revealed that the entropy loss resulting from this phenomenon is a concave function, which can be minimized by selecting specific threshold values. By applying this understanding, we derived a key rate expression for QKD systems that incorporate non-uniform random seeds. Our results indicate that the effect of entropy loss is most pronounced in low-entropy seeds and can be mitigated by implementing a dual-phase coding approach.

A curve $\gamma$ in a semi-metric space is considered a Bertrand curve if its osculating plane at each point coincides with the osculating plane of another given curve $\beta$.  Two curves are considered Bertrand counterparts if they satisfy this condition.  This article explores properties of a particular class of Bertrand curves, specifically those whose osculating planes coincide with the osculating planes of plane curves (one-dimensional subspaces in $\Bbb R^3$).  It is shown that for such curves, the normal direction is fixed and they can be considered as "spatial curves" regardless of the underlying space.  The article also examines the relationship between Bertrand curves and a particular alignment of tangent and normal vectors.

We examine the properties of a class of stochastic processes, known as Feller processes, which serve as the basis for the coalescent, a tool used to model the ancestral histories of genes. This work aims to understand the relationship between the process and its corresponding sampling distribution, which describes the genetic diversity of a population. To achieve this, we develop a probabilistic framework that links the process to the sampling distribution. This framework enables us to determine the conditions under which the process generates a valid, genealogical coalescent. Furthermore, we derive sampling distributions from non-Markovian processes, which serve as the fundamental models for various demographic scenarios.

In our research, we've developed a new method for analyzing the scattering behavior of multi-photon states in waveguide QED systems. By using this approach, we can graphically represent and compute the S-matrix for any given interaction potential, which allows us to determine the scattering cross-section and rates for multi-photon states. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this method by applying it to various scenarios, including the scattering of two and three photons off a single atom, the photoassociative scattering of two atoms, and the scattering of three photons off two atoms. We've also shown that our method can reproduce the results obtained through traditional diagrammatic techniques and recent exact numerical calculations.

We investigate dark matter's interaction with a black hole by considering the effects of spin-dependent interactions. By using the S-wave approximation, we derived a set of cross-section equations for non-relativistic dark matter, which can be applied to various black hole models. Our analysis also takes into account the effects of acceleration, finding that the cross-sections are generally reduced when the black hole's acceleration is in the same direction as its spin. Furthermore, we found that the cross-sections are sensitive to the parameters of the Yukawa coupling, particularly for low-mass dark matter.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

In conventional non-coherent differential continuous-phase modulation (CPM) detection, additional processing is necessary to mitigate the effects of unknown phase and amplitude, resulting in a delay in the detection process. This delay is influenced by the duration of the received signal block and the CPM parameters. To minimize the impact of this delay, a lower block size is typically employed, but this also increases the variability of the detection metric. This work examines the causes of the delay in non-coherent differential CPM detection and presents an analytical model to estimate it. The delay is found to be particularly significant for CPM formats with high values of two-slope roll-off factor alpha and bandwidth efficiency.

Reward functions in reinforcement learning often require extensive data and time to determine, but in our research, we've developed a method to significantly speed up this process using human feedback. Our approach involves dividing the reward function space into groups and asking experts to categorize these clusters, which enables more efficient learning. By using visual aids and minimizing the need for detailed policy training, we've created a reward learning technique that is faster and more practical for human experts to use. Our experiments show that this method can learn effective rewards in half the time compared to traditional approaches.

Utilizing the light-front quark-diquark model, our investigation of nucleon structure properties on light-front quantum field theory framework within noncommutative space-time reveals that the nucleon's constituent quark and gluon momentum distributions, helicity distributions, and orbital angular momentum alignments are significantly impacted by noncommutative geometry effects. Notably, the noncommutativity influences on these distributions are distinct for quarks and gluons. Moreover, the orbital angular momentum of gluons in a nucleon is found to be sensitive to noncommutativity, which may provide valuable insights into the nucleon's gluon orbital angular momentum alignments.

We investigate the effects of geometric frustration on the Toric code, a topological quantum code designed to operate on a dually connected surface, modified to include a non-Planar, irregularly structured lattice. Within this framework, a non-geometrically encoded 'kite' element is introduced, which, when decoded, yields a geometric line without the ability to encode a logical qubit, due to the absence of dual vertices, thus preventing a non-trivial encoded state. Despite this limitation, a geometric 'kite' still facilitates the transfer of a physical qubit between distant points through the assistance of multiple gates. Furthermore, the presence of geometric lines also enables the verification of quantum errors through the measurement of the mutual information between the code blocks, thus serving as a quantum error detection method.

We investigate the eigenvalue behavior of finite-rank modifications to large random matrices, specifically in the Hermitian and real symmetric domains. Our analysis reveals that the statistical properties of eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors can be effectively approximated by a specific statistical model. This model consists of two distinct components: a Gaussian matrix variation and a rank-one matrix containing the eigenvector's phase components. Our findings are supported by a rigorous mathematical derivation, which involves a specific statistical model and a generalization of the Jensen's inequality for free additive Brownian motions.

Recent breakthroughs in conversational AI have been largely attributed to pre-trained language models (PLMs), which have significantly accelerated the development of dialogue systems. However, current dialogue PLMs primarily rely on sequence-to-sequence learning and fall short in addressing critical dialogue understanding tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel meaning-based pre-training framework, which leverages semantic parsing to capture the underlying meaning of input text and distill key concepts essential for dialogue comprehension. Our approach comprises two stages: (1) meaning-based BERT pre-training, which utilizes a customized semantic parsing head to refine BERT's representation of input text, and (2) fine-tuning for downstream dialogue understanding tasks. Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance across a range of benchmarks, outperforming existing dialogue PLMs and yielding consistent improvements in multiple evaluation metrics.

Deep neural networks have achieved impressive accuracy on a wide range of tasks, but their complex decision-making processes are difficult for humans to understand.  In order to improve their performance in real-world applications, it's crucial to make them more 'interpretable', i.e., able to explain their predictions and decisions in a way that's easy for humans to understand.  However, there's no widely accepted definition of interpretability, and current methods for measuring it are limited.  In this study, we propose a new approach to assess algorithmic interpretability based on how well a learner can learn from a model's explanations of its decisions and predictions.  We developed a cognitive complexity score to evaluate how easy it is for humans to learn from different models, and we tested it using explanations from several machine learning models in the fields of vision and language.  Our results show that this new approach provides a more accurate and meaningful measure of interpretability than existing methods, and it's also more effective at identifying models that are easier for humans to learn from.

The increasing complexity of Machine Learning models has led to a growing need for models that can execute quickly without hindering performance.  Isolation Forest, a simple yet efficient algorithm, excels at anomaly detection with a low computational footprint.  This paper presents an optimized version of the Isolation Forest, leveraging the Ti-WS framework to enhance its performance on edge devices.  The TiWS-IForest implementation yields a significant speedup over the original Isolation Forest, while requiring minimal additional memory.

A novel approach utilizing a Poisson process reparameterization transforms the modeling of extreme events into a more manageable Poisson regression problem, facilitating the use of Bayesian inference techniques. This method enables the calculation of extreme event occurrence probabilities, as well as the estimation of extreme event thresholds and associated uncertainty. The approach is versatile and can be applied to both temporal and spatial data sets, as well as data that exhibits non-stationarity or non-constant extreme event behavior. The approach is validated through a case study of extreme rainfall in the city of Melbourne, Australia, as well as a spatial analysis of extreme flooding in the city of London, UK.

In nonstandard models, the average cross section can be either positive or negative. To identify areas meeting specific criteria, we'll use a method called partitioning, dividing the model space into distinct sections based on different conditions. By analyzing these partitions, we can pinpoint areas where the average cross section meets certain requirements. Our research focuses on two types of regions: those where the average cross section is fixed at zero and those where it's fixed at a specific, non-zero value.

The COMET-ATOMIC dataset is a comprehensive knowledge base consisting of 4000 natural language descriptions related to 400 causal events. It encompasses 12 distinct atomic actions and their corresponding subatomic components, which are used to describe the cause, manner, and effect of these events. This dataset serves as a foundation for understanding complex causal relationships. In this study, we examine the current state of machine representation of this knowledge graph using symbolic and neural approaches. We propose a novel task to assess the ability of these representations to predict the subatomic components of events. We also develop a benchmark consisting of 1000 questions that target specific aspects of the COMET-ATOMIC knowledge graph. This benchmark serves as a standardized evaluation tool for future research and is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/COMET-ATOMIC-Benchmark.

The data from the Hi-GAL survey, which is part of the Herschel SPIRE Guaranteed Time Mission, has been processed through a series of steps to prepare the data for the public release. This processing involved multiple stages including data reduction, map creation, and data compression. The data compression stage utilized multiple techniques, including filtering and lossless compression, to achieve optimal results. The final compressed data, which is available at 350, 500, and 2100 micron wavelengths, can be decompressed using the provided tools to restore the original data in its raw format.

The metal-poor globular cluster NGC 2808 is of particular interest due to its distinct stellar subpopulations, which are thought to represent the initial chemical composition of the galaxy. By analyzing high-resolution spectra of 16 bright red giant stars within the cluster, we have determined the abundance of key chemical elements in NGC 2808. Our analysis reveals a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] = -1.63 +/- 0.04, which is consistent with a small spread of +/- 0.10. This result is in agreement with a previous study and confirms the presence of multiple stellar subgroups with distinct metal abundances.

We investigate the characteristics of the initial exit time from a confined area in single file diffusion, employing a semi-finite domain as a model of enclosure. The mean initial exit time is determined analytically for a semi-finite domain and numerically for a more complex, semi-enclosed region. The distribution of the initial exit time is also examined. The findings suggest that entropic repulsive forces play a crucial role in facilitating the initial exit process.

Quantum Mechanics' measurement outcome predictions pose an inference problem, as they rely on the quantum state of an unmeasured system. To address this issue, we apply Bayes' Rule within the context of Quantum Mechanics, using the quantum version of Bayes' Rule. This approach yields two key findings. Firstly, it shows that the quantum state can remain consistent throughout a sequence of measurements. Secondly, it demonstrates that the quantum state's transformation during measurement, known as wavefunction collapse, is not a fundamental change, but rather a consequence of considering only the relevant information from each measurement.

We apply the equation of state for QCD to small, non-central collision systems, assuming a thermal state that's perturbatively calculable. We derive an equation that relates the average number of charged particles to the average transverse momentum, and use it to fit data from CMS and ATLAS at 7 and 13 TeV. Our approach yields a well-fitting equation of state that's insensitive to specific thermal models, and allows us to determine system size and calculate transport coefficients.

In the realm of infinite dimensional Lie algebras, a distinct subcategory emerges, characterized by the presence of a finite dimensional Lie algebra structure. This unique property is akin to a linear representation in the Steenrod algebra, albeit one that is not necessarily finite dimensional. This work aims to explore the cohomology of such representations, with a specific focus on the non-trivial elements within these cohomology groups.

Astronomers studying the universe's formation and evolution are hindered by the Earth's atmosphere blocking most of its light, making it necessary to conduct observations from space-based platforms. However, the interstellar medium contains neutral hydrogen that absorbs the Lyman series, rendering it impossible to conduct certain observations without a suitable filter. Researchers have developed a Lyman-alpha filter prototype capable of passing Lyman series wavelengths while blocking surrounding continuum and Balmer series emissions. The filter's unique design, featuring a thin layer of aluminum, achieves this specificity by utilizing interference effects. The prototype's effectiveness was tested by analyzing spectra of white dwarf stars and a supernova remnant, and the results demonstrate its ability to block Balmer series emissions while transmitting Lyman series wavelengths.

This research focuses on developing scalable management strategies for graph-based systems, specifically those requiring synchronization or coordination among nodes. Graph filters, a time-domain extension of traditional frequency-domain filters, offer an efficient solution for distributed control and management. By leveraging the properties of graph shift operators, it is possible to design effective communication protocols that balance the trade-off between control efficiency and communication overhead. The paper demonstrates this concept through the analysis of two key systems: node synchronization and target tracking. Synchronization is achieved by designing a filter that amplifies frequency components, then utilizing the graph shift operator to disseminate this information to all nodes. The target tracking system, on the other hand, involves a filter that amplifies the target's spectral representation, then utilizes the graph shift operator to direct communication towards the target node.

This paper introduces a novel technique for rapidly searching and retrieving images from a database based on their visual characteristics. The proposed method employs a data structure that enables efficient indexing of images by their visual attributes, allowing for various image descriptors to be utilized. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique using a database of 1 million images, indexed using a combination of SIFT and deep learning descriptors. The method is then applied to a large-scale image retrieval task, where it is compared to other state-of-the-art techniques. The results show that the proposed technique can significantly reduce the time it takes to search for images, with an average speed-up of 10 times or more, depending on the specific image descriptor used.

A physical layer-based approach to authenticate wireless communications is proposed, which relies solely on the receiver's physical layer capabilities and doesn't require additional hardware or software components. This method exploits the inherent randomness in wireless channels to generate and verify unique codes for each transmission session. The codes are generated at the transmitter using channel state estimation and the receiver confirms authenticity by checking that the received message matches the expected code. The theoretical framework for this method is established by analyzing a binary symmetric channel, and it's shown that as the transmission size increases, the probability of authentic and non-authentic messages approaches 1/2. The performance of this method is evaluated through simulations, and it's found that it can achieve a high level of security, surpassing existing physical layer security methods.

We examine the movement of a particle in a washboard potential, a nonlinear perturbation of the linear potential. This particle's motion is characterized by a specific point, the critical inflection point, where its velocity deviates from linearity. Our objective is to determine whether this deviation affects its asymptotic linearity. To achieve this, we apply a technique that reduces the nonlinear problem to a related linear problem at a particular stage. By linking the two problems, we demonstrate the existence of a solution that remains linearly dependent on position. Consequently, the particle's motion is a combination of linear and periodic components, where the superposition of these components remains constant over time.

This research introduces a dynamic forecasting framework, capable of handling complex data relationships, to predict short-term and long-term impacts following unexpected events. The proposed model, built on a structured equation framework, incorporates an immediate response mechanism and a separate equation for modeling post-crisis phenomena. Results from applying this model to data on stock market reactions to major crises in the 21st century demonstrate its ability to accurately forecast both immediate and subsequent market responses to future crises.

The angular Casimir force between two cylindrical objects, each carrying an electric charge and rotating around a common axis, is examined in the context of the quantum vacuum. This force has a component that acts as a torque, causing the axes of the cylinders to precess. An expression for this torque has been derived and quantified, and its properties have been explored in greater detail. Notably, the torque is influenced by the geometric and topological characteristics of the objects in question, specifically by the area-to-circumference ratio of the cylinders and the presence of holes. This investigation also reveals that the torque is contingent upon the relative orientations of the objects' rotational axes, as well as the presence of magnetic dipole moments.

The success of named entity recognition in languages with limited data and complex structures depends on the performance of the model's entity classification, which is often achieved through the use of convolutional neural networks or recurrent models. However, these models struggle to handle the challenges posed by languages with limited data and complex structures. To address these challenges, a new approach called FGNET-RH has been developed, which uses a hierarchical refinement of hyperbolic networks to improve the accuracy of named entity recognition. The model consists of two main components: a coarse-grained network that performs initial entity classification and a fine-grained network that refines the classification by leveraging contextual information. The model's performance is evaluated using the F1-score metric on six datasets, which include languages with limited data and complex structures, as well as English text. The results show that FGNET-RH outperforms state-of-the-art models, including CNN and RNN-based models, as well as other hyperbolic network models, achieving an average improvement of 0.8 and 1.1 points in F1-score, respectively.

This paper provides explicit formulas for the second Hankel determinant for the special class $\mathcal{U}$ and the general class $\mathcal{S}$, expressing the results using iterated integrals and the Vasil'ev integral.

In a cloud data center, virtualized resources are allocated to users as virtual machines. To prevent service disruptions, administrators must ensure timely response times by managing traffic and network bandwidth. This paper proposes the Prepartition approach to distribute network traffic and prevent over-subscription, thereby enabling real-time network Quality of Service (QoS) guarantees for critical applications. Prepartition involves partitioning physical switches into virtual sub-switches, each managing its own traffic and preventing data collisions. This approach achieves high performance, scalability, and efficiency, with fast setup and tear-down times. Evaluations using real-world traffic show that Prepartition outperforms existing solutions in terms of network traffic, switch memory, and network delay.

We introduce a novel approach to forecast the evolution of dynamical systems
that involve multiple interacting agents, where each agent adjusts its state based
on a fixed point calculation. Our method, Fixed Point Networks, leverages the
insights gained from the theory of equilibrium systems, enabling it to capture
the long-term behavior of these systems. Fixed Point Networks achieve state-of-the-art
performance in predicting the eventual equilibrium of these systems, surpassing
other state-of-the-art models, according to evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we
demonstrate that Fixed Point Networks can successfully forecast the trajectory
of these systems over time, even when the system is highly nonlinear and
interconnected.

In many fields, including medicine, biology, and engineering, it's often necessary to analyze complex systems involving numerous variables. These systems can be viewed as networks where variables interact and influence each other. This raises questions about how one variable might affect another, and whether such influence is direct or indirect. To address these concerns, we develop a mathematical approach to quantify the impact of one variable on another, and test it on large datasets. This method enables us to identify causal relationships and determine the strength of such relationships. By applying this approach to genetic data, we can identify genes that may affect other genes, and also examine its effectiveness on synthetic data and real-world medical datasets.

This study proposes an efficient method for early detection of covert attacks on LTI systems using only normal operating data. The proposed method relies on a new, simple feature that measures the distance between the system's predicted and actual behaviors. It uses a single offline linear model to forecast the system's trajectory under normal conditions and then calculates the distance to the actual trajectory in real-time. The distance threshold is set based on historical data to trigger an alarm. The method's performance is evaluated using simulated data from a power grid system, demonstrating its ability to detect stealthy cyber attacks up to 10 seconds in advance.

A document summary is a condensed version, created to represent the original text, which can be generated through automatic summarization. This process, typically a difficult task for computers, is made more manageable by employing a model that leverages a summary's inherent structure. Graph-based automatic summarization models, which treat a summary as a connected network of key sentences, have shown promise in improving summary quality. Our research introduces GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised Indian language graph-based automatic summaration model that uses a unique scoring method to produce high-quality summaries. By combining a key-sentence extraction algorithm with a ranking procedure, GAE-ISumm effectively generates summaries, which we have validated through experiments on real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that GAE-ISumm outperforms existing methods in terms of ROUGE score.

We establish that for a ring R with 1, if every right ideal of R is
Cohen to some left ideal, then R itself is Cohen to some left ideal. This
result expands on a finding by K. R. Baith and S. P. Chakraborty. Furthermore,
we demonstrate that for a ring R with 1, the presence of S-rings, a type of
Cohen subrings, implies the existence of left ideals that are also S-rings. This
outcome generalizes an observation made by S. P. Chakraborty and T. K. Gupta.
Additionally, we show that for a ring R with 1, the presence of S-rings
corresponds to the existence of left ideals that are quasi-monomial in R. This
result expands on an observation made by S. P. Chakraborty and T. K. Gupta.

Recent studies have revealed a mysterious acceleration in the movement of several nearby young stars.  Researchers have proposed that this phenomenon could be attributed to the gravitational pull from unseen companions.  To explore this hypothesis, a statistical analysis was conducted to examine the likelihood of a massive companion affecting the stars' motion.  The study focused on five stars that exhibited detectable acceleration and used radial velocity curves to search for companions.  The results showed that the presence of a companion with a mass greater than 10 Jupiter masses could be detected with high confidence levels, especially at close distances.  However, the statistical evidence did not provide strong support for the presence of such a companion.  The study's findings suggest that the gravitational pull from a massive companion is unlikely to explain the observed acceleration in the stars' motion.  The study's results are consistent with the stars' motion being random, and the acceleration could be attributed to various random factors.

We introduce the LSVAE, a novel autoencoder model that employs a least squares objective function and incorporates a variational Bayesian framework. The LSVAE is characterized by an encoder and decoder network that share a common distributional parameter, allowing for a unified approach to learning the model's parameters. The LSVAE utilizes a variational approach to account for uncertainty in the model, with the objective function optimized through a combination of evidence lower bound maximization and regularization terms. The LSVAE is a versatile framework that can be applied to a range of network configurations, including both supervised and self-supervised learning scenarios. The model's performance is evaluated through a series of image reconstruction tasks, with the results indicating that LSVAE achieves superior reconstruction quality and scale flexibility compared to existing approaches.

Smart home devices are increasingly being connected to the internet, which has led to a growing concern about their security. As these devices are now vulnerable to cyber threats, it's essential to develop a reliable method for detecting and preventing malicious activities. This research aims to address this issue by creating an intelligent system for identifying and tracking IoT devices. The proposed system utilizes a private blockchain to securely monitor and locate IoT devices, which can be implemented on a smart home network. By analyzing data from various sources, including device sensors and user behavior, the system can accurately detect anomalies and detect potential cyber threats.

This research introduces a novel approach to gray-code modulation by dividing the signal's Gray map into distinct segments with unique slopes. The quantization of each slope is performed using a neural network-based model, which is trained on real-world communication systems' datasets. By applying this model to multiple slopes, a modulation scheme with enhanced error performance and increased bit density is achieved. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional approaches, with significant reductions in error rates and increased bit density for various modulation types.

This study introduces novel algorithmic techniques to solve an up to $k$-planarity issue, which involves determining if a directed graph can be divided into $k$ or fewer planar subgraphs. The paper presents a linear-time algorithm for recognizing if a directed graph can be broken down into $k$ planar subgraphs and, in $O(k^5.5\polylog k)$ time, it can identify a specific division of the graph into $k$ planar subgraphs. Additionally, the study shows that for a specific class of graphs, which are acyclic, the problem of identifying a specific division of the graph into $k$ planar subgraphs can be solved in $O(k^{2.5}\polylog k)$ time.

Crowdsourcing has become a standard approach for gathering ground truth labels for image classification tasks, but it's often hindered by inaccuracies due to crowdworkers' varying levels of expertise and attention to detail.  This study proposes a method to account for this noise by utilizing crowdsourcing to gather multiple labels per image.  By combining these labels with a Bayesian neural network, trained as an ensemble, the method can accurately predict its own uncertainty, allowing it to filter out noisy labels and produce more accurate results.  The study also explores the effect of human bias on the model by analyzing the 'human softmax' distributions, which reveal patterns of class bias.  By incorporating entropic metrics of uncertainty, the method can detect images with high uncertainty and exclude them from the dataset.  The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach on the ImageNet dataset, achieving state-of-the-art performance without relying on pre-training.

We develop a method to assess the effectiveness of abstract approximation operators in approximating linear systems, which can be applied to both discrete and continuous systems. This is achieved by establishing a bound on the norm of the transfer operator in the $\mathscr{L}(\ell^2,\mathbb{C})$ space. This operator's norm is a measure of the spectral radius, which in turn indicates the existence of invariant measures under the semiflow. This work is a continuation of our previous research on finite-state systems, which we now extend to infinite-state systems. We apply our method to two distinct examples: a piecewise contraction with a periodic boundary condition and a piecewise contraction with a stable equilibrium.

This research introduces a novel algorithm for creating $g$-symbol strength-$2$ covering arrays of size $n \times m$, particularly those with $g \leq 15$. The algorithm yields arrays with reduced sizes compared to existing methods, as demonstrated through numerous examples. The resulting arrays also meet the parameters specified in the literature exactly, rather than approximations used in previous approaches.

We demonstrate that for any desired level of precision, it is possible to determine whether a nonlocal game utilizing an n-dimensional maximally correlated state, affected by random errors, can be achieved. This is done by attributing the referee's decision-making process to a new game called the 'identification game', which involves players A and B attempting to identify the binary vector representing the measurement outcomes from the original game. Since the original game can be achieved if and only if the identification game can, and since random errors on high-dimensional states do not significantly impact their ability to achieve nonlocal games, it follows that the original game can be achieved if and only if the identification game can. Furthermore, the identification game can be achieved with a level of certainty that approaches 1 as the number of desired precision steps increases.

In software engineering, generating automated test case reproductions for crashes is a critical issue with many applications. This issue is particularly challenging due to the inherent complexity and unknown nature of program states at the time of a crash. The application of evolutionary algorithms in this context has shown significant potential, with some studies yielding impressive results. However, the field still faces several unresolved challenges. This study aims to build on existing research by replicating and adapting the findings of a previous study, focusing on the guided genetic algorithm approach. By examining the underlying causes of crashes, this approach aims to produce test case reproductions. Our replication of the study involved using the Java Pathfinder tool to investigate the reproduction of crashes in three open-source Java applications. The results of our experiments revealed that the guided genetic algorithm was unable to produce test case reproductions for two applications, while only succeeding in one. Notably, the algorithm's performance was hindered by the presence of multiple crash causes and the difficulty of identifying these causes.

The arrangement of magnetic vortices in superconductors near their critical temperature reveals the underlying structure of superconducting fluctuations. In the vicinity of the critical point, the typical square pattern of magnetic vortices transforms into a grid-like structure at low magnetic fields. Our research on the square-grid transition in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.50}$ shows that it occurs at a temperature of $T^* = 55.5$ K, where the grid-like structure persists in the absence of magnetic fields. This transition is characterized by a distinct change in the superconducting fluctuations, as evidenced by specific heat measurements. Our findings suggest that the square-grid transition is a distinct phase transition in high-temperature cuprate superconductors.

The early universe was a hot, dense, and dynamic state known as the quark-gluon plasma (sQGP), in which particles were moving freely and interacting with each other. By studying this state under controlled conditions at RHIC, researchers can gain valuable insights into the fundamental nature of matter. In this research, we investigate how photons, which can travel long distances without being affected, move within the sQGP. By analyzing their movement patterns, we can gain a deeper understanding of the sQGP's properties. Our findings reveal that thermal photons exhibit complex movement patterns that are influenced by the non-uniform conditions within the sQGP. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the non-uniform movement patterns of photons are directly linked to the sQGP's viscosity, serving as a sensitive probe of its properties.

We investigate the possibility of common magnetic orders in triangular and
kagome lattices that share a vertex-only coupling. Our research reveals that for
such systems, the ground states are either all-zero magnetization or feature the
same non-zero magnetization orientation in both sublattices. Moreover, we've
derived a set of rules governing the emergence of these common magnetic orders
and found that they are highly resistant to minor lattice distortions. These
results are supported by numerical simulations on a triangular-kagome system
coupled by frustrated interactions.

We address a critical issue in large-scale experimentation, which involves detecting treatment effects at controlled false discovery rates, even when data points are interdependent. Traditional methods rely on assumptions of independence or weak correlations, but these are often unrealistic in modern settings. To overcome this challenge, we propose a new approach that leverages a multi-stage screening and thresholding strategy, combined with an innovative dependence-aware p-value adjustment. Through theoretical analysis and simulation, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method in controlling the family-wise error rate and discovering treatment effects, while also outperforming existing alternatives in real-world conditions.

The universe's expansion is observed to be uniform in all directions, with most evidence pointing to it being flat and homogeneous. The majority of the universe's matter is thought to be composed of dark energy, with the cosmological constant being a potential candidate to explain this phenomenon. In this context, the universe's expansion is often described using the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker model, which suggests that the scale factor's rate of change is constant over time. However, there are also theories proposing that the universe's expansion is not uniformly consistent in all directions, with some models even suggesting that the scale factor's rate of change can vary over time.

The CERN experiment's measurement of the muon's magnetic moment shows a significant discrepancy from the Standard Model's predictions, equivalent to about 4 sigma. A similar anomaly is observed in the mass of the W boson, with a discrepancy of around 6 sigma. In this study, a type-X two Higgs doublet model is examined to see if it can account for both the muon's anomalous magnetic moment and the W boson's mass issues simultaneously. The type-X 2HDM has an advantage over other 2HDM types in this regard, as it doesn't have restrictions on the Higgs boson mass, making it easier to fit the observed values of the muon's magnetic moment and the W boson's mass.

When developers use search engines to find relevant information, they often reformulate their queries based on the initial results, taking advantage of feedback provided by the system. This process, known as query reformulation, is also applied in the concept location task, where software engineers adapt their search queries to obtain more suitable results. Despite its importance, the underlying motivations and methods driving this adaptation are not well understood. Our research proposes a new approach called QUICKAR, which uses crowd-sourced information to discover relationships between search terms and related concepts, enabling more effective reformulation of queries to improve concept location. The technique involves a learning algorithm that identifies key modifications to improve search results, and our experiments demonstrate its potential benefits.

In interactions between people, the practice of mirroring each other's communication patterns, known as entrainment, plays a significant role in demonstrating understanding and building connections. While previous studies on entrainment have been limited due to the labor-intensive process of manually annotating data, this research aims to develop an automated method for measuring entrainment in spoken conversations. By applying a data-driven approach using deep neural networks, this study investigates whether the characteristics of speech can be used to identify entrainment. To this end, a new metric called "Conversational Entrainment Index" (CEI) is proposed, which assesses the level of entrainment between interlocutors based on their use of pauses, speech rate, and language patterns. By training a CEI model using artificially created data with annotated entrainment labels, this study demonstrates its effectiveness in accurately predicting entrainment in both simulated and real-world conversations.

The second iteration of the RCSED project introduces a pair of open-source web applications built with Flask, a Python web framework. These tools, comprising rcSEDv2-Viewer and rcSEDv2-Analyzer, enable users to visualize and generate spectral or spatial representations of galaxies through various interactive tools, including a viewer and a spectrometer model analyzer. The rcSEDv2-Viewer allows users to view and download 1D, 2D, or 3D spectral or spatial representations of galaxies, while the rcSEDv2-Analyzer offers a range of spectrometer models to simulate and analyze observations. The tools are accessible online at http://rcsedv2.cosmicdawn.org.

Temporal action segmentation, a task of identifying discrete actions within continuous videos, typically relies on well-annotated datasets. However, manual segmentation and labeling are labor-intensive and often impractical. This paper presents a novel approach to tackle temporal action segmentation without relying on annotated datasets. This method, called Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Prediction (SSCAP), uses self-supervised learning to create pseudo-labels for individual actions and their co-occurrences. A two-stream model then utilizes these pseudo-labels to segment actions in test videos. SSCAP demonstrates superior performance on Kinetics400, Breakfast, 50Salads, and HumanEva, outperforming unsupervised baselines and comparable supervised methods.

In the context of the diquark model, we examine the properties of hidden-charm pentaquark states and their connections to $D$-meson pairs. We then investigate the production of $D\bar{D}^*$, $D^* \bar{D}^*$, and $D D^\ast$ meson pairs in nucleon processes, as well as the decays of $P_c^+$ pentaquark states to $D\bar{D}^*$, $D^* \bar{D}^*$, and $D D^\ast$. We also explore the existence of $P_c^-$ pentaquark states and their associated decays.

The traditional approach to providing feedback to students in software testing education can be overly critical and may lead to students developing a fear of testing, which hinders their ability to learn and grow. To address this issue, we conducted an empirical study to compare the effectiveness of two types of feedback: a comprehensive, detailed approach and an inquiry-based, conceptual approach. The goal of this study was to identify which type of feedback is more beneficial for students and how it impacts their learning outcomes. By analyzing the data collected from a survey and an experiment involving 54 students, we found that students generally prefer conceptual feedback and tend to perform better when provided with such feedback. The empirical results also revealed that conceptual feedback is more beneficial for students in terms of their understanding of testing principles and their overall confidence in their abilities.

Domain adaptation challenges traditional methods by removing access to the source domain's training data. To overcome this limitation, we propose Hypothesis Shift, a novel approach that adapts to a target domain using pre-trained models and diverse initial hypotheses on the target domain. Our method allows the incorporation of multiple hypotheses, enhancing the potential for successful adaptation. Furthermore, Hypothesis Shift can be combined with semi-supervised learning to improve adaptation even with limited target label information. Through comprehensive evaluations on various adaptation tasks, Hypothesis Shift demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

A novel approach to deep space propulsion, the gas core engine, has been gaining attention in recent years. This propulsion system operates by maintaining a plasma core within a closed chamber, allowing for the collection of electrical energy through an external magnetic field. This engine is seen as a potential alternative to traditional chemical rockets for interplanetary travel. This study aims to provide an overview of the gas core engine's basic principles, its various configurations, and the current advancements in the field.

A novel neural network approach has been developed for localizing air showers in astroparticle experiments, leveraging the synergy between neural networks and domain knowledge. By incorporating geometric constraints and selecting optimal coordinate systems, this method minimizes positional ambiguity and enhances localization precision. The proposed framework is adaptable to various detector configurations and can be applied to diverse particle rates, ranging from single-event to real-time tracking. The technique is illustrated using the HiCal air shower experiment's data, achieving a positional resolution of 10 meters in three dimensions.

We introduce EXOPLINES, a comprehensive database of absorption coefficients for molecules relevant to the atmospheres of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets. This database bridges the knowledge gap for species lacking existing absorption data, thereby facilitating the development of more accurate radiative transfer codes for low-temperature atmospheres. EXOPLINES provides a unified resource for absorption data across diverse temperature ranges, enabling researchers to model various atmospheric environments. We discuss the implementation of our data and its potential applications, including the generation of synthetic spectra and the analysis of observed spectra, as well as the expansion of EXOPLINES to include additional species and temperature ranges.

Answer set programming offers a computational framework for addressing intricate
logical inquiries via a declarative approach. However, the ambiguity inherent in natural
language necessitates additional context for pinpointing specific inquiries. Grounding
provides a way to link abstract statements to concrete facts, which can be utilized both for
understanding natural language inquiries and grounding them. Despite its significance, the
principles underlying grounding have not been thoroughly explored. This study aims to fill
this gap by outlining the fundamental principles of grounding in answer set programming,
including the creation of grounded atoms and models, and examining their connections to
existing paradigms.

We establish a fundamental principle for the initial state in a general quantum resource theory, which is based on a key assumption that for any resource R, its initial abundance cannot decrease over time. This principle leads to the discovery of a non-decreasing, convex cone of resource non-negative operators, enabling the characterization of the initial state as the only state that remains resource non-decreasing under unitary evolution. Additionally, this principle provides a natural definition for the resource rate class, which is a closed and bounded set within the state space.

We develop a statistical framework to analyze a stochastic process by leveraging information in its moment dynamics. This involves modeling a sequence of information vectors, each containing a function of a random variable, ordered by decreasing information content. We establish a general framework for such sequences, define a subclass that is information-theoretically sound, and provide a method to measure a stochastic process using only moment sequences that belong to this subclass. We also show that this measurement aligns with the minimum amount of information needed to achieve a desired level of performance in hypothesis testing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through experiments involving binary and multi-class classification tasks, and show that it outperforms existing methods in various scenarios.

In a multivariate time series with non-fixed covariance, heavy-tailed noise, and a constant matrix, we developed a method to estimate the inverse of the noise covariance. This estimator has an asymptotic normal distribution and performed well in simulations, outperforming other techniques. This method has potential applications in a related problem where we need to make inferences about the mean of a multivariate time series with similar noise characteristics.

We've developed a new class of quantum low-density parity-check codes that can be efficiently decoded in linear time. These codes are based on a specific construction involving classical LDPC codes with particular structural characteristics. We've also devised a message-passing decoding algorithm that can be applied universally, achieving a threshold error rate. Furthermore, we've established that the decoding process for this code exhibits a characteristic known as sublinear mixing, which is a critical factor in determining the code's error rate. We've also demonstrated that the code's error rate is directly influenced by the code's spectral gap and the code's density, which is a measure of the code's connectivity.

A $r$-dominating set of a graph, known as a distance-$r$ dominating set, with respect to a given vertex in a graph, is a subset of vertices that ensures every vertex in the graph is within a distance of $r$ from at least one vertex in the subset. The concept of a group dominating set was first introduced in 2011 by Fomin et al. and has been further developed in the context of making locally consistent $r$-dominating sets of graph, and specifically the problem of finding a group $\rho$-dominating set in time $O(\rho \cdot n^{1+\epsilon})$ for any constant $\epsilon > 0$. In this paper, we present a distributed algorithm that finds a distance-$r$ dominating group $\rho$-dominating set in time $O(\rho \log^2 n)$ for any graph with a constant average degree and a girth of at least $r+3$.

We investigate the bulk-surface correspondence in disordered higher-order topological insulators with non-trivial properties on multiple boundaries. Focusing on a 2D model with two-fold rotational symmetry, our analysis reveals that the bulk and surface characteristics are connected through a robust surface mode, which persists even in the presence of disorder. The bulk-surface correspondence is facilitated by a surface Dirac cone with anisotropic velocities. The velocity anisotropy arises from disorder-induced intermixing of different surface states, which does not occur in clean systems. The bulk-surface correspondence is stable across various types of disorder and does not rely on the disorder average. The findings can be extended to other higher-order topological insulators in different dimensions.

The CMS experiment's search for supersymmetry is a top priority, with a comprehensive approach to exploring the vast SUSY parameter space across various supersymmetry models. This research presents the latest findings from multiple searches for new, heavy particles that are predicted by supersymmetry, with a focus on final states containing large jet multiplicity and missing transverse momentum. The results are based on 137 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at the LHC, with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The research examines the potential of these searches to make significant contributions to the ongoing search for supersymmetry, with a focus on final states containing multiple b-quarks.

Recent advancements in neural rendering have shown significant promise in creating realistic 3D visual effects, yet most existing methods are limited to using specific colored light sources or rely on pre-rendered images. Our novel approach, bright field neural rendering, enables the creation of realistic 3D scenes using only the interaction of ambient light and without the use of light sources. By training a neural network to generate 3D scenes from 2D images and object poses, and using a novel loss function, we can accurately recreate the way light interacts with objects in the scene. Furthermore, our method can be easily extended to create realistic 3D animations by training a neural network to predict object movements. Our results demonstrate the potential of our approach in creating highly realistic 3D scenes and animations using only ambient light.

The data comprise 222 sets of observations from 87 systems, yielding 163 resolved pairs and 59 non-resolved pairs. The results include angular separations, separation changes, and mass ratios for 59 pairs, along with the discovery of 13 new binary systems. The data also include resolved pairs with orbital periods less than one year, and the results include updated orbital periods and eccentricities for 16 pairs. The results also include the determination of minimum masses for 48 pairs, and the results include the discovery of 11 low-mass stars as companions. We explore the properties of a class of celestial algebras with chiral characteristics and their associated quantum groups. By applying the WZNW formulation, we derive a novel integrable system on the plane. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the proposed system and a well-known model through the construction of a duality transformation. This transformation reveals the existence of a dual integrable system, and through the application of the gauge equivalent transformation, we link it to the self-dual model.

A solar piston blast is triggered by a coronal mass ejection pushing into the lower atmosphere, causing shock waves to form in the chromosphere and low corona. Researchers have observed this phenomenon using the LOFAR radio telescope, which detected the piston blast at multiple frequencies and detected a type II and type III radio burst. The type II burst showed a characteristic forward and reverse shock structure, indicating that the blast was triggered by a coronal mass ejection propagating at high speeds. The type III burst was likely generated by a beam of energetic particles traveling along magnetic field lines towards the observer. The piston blast was observed to be highly dynamic, with the shock waves moving at high speeds and the CME driving the process. The researchers used the LOFAR data to create a 3D model of the piston blast, which showed that the piston was located at the base of the shock and the CME was propagating at high speeds above. The study demonstrates the capabilities of LOFAR for observing low-frequency radio bursts from the piston blast and provides valuable insights into the physics of this phenomenon.

The general two Higgs doublet model is examined in the context of several observed anomalies in particle interactions, specifically those related to $b\to c$ and $b\to s$ decays, the decay of the tau lepton, the decay of the bottom quark, and the particle known as the muon. A comprehensive analysis of the model's potential solutions to these anomalies is presented, and the model's predictions for several key particle properties are made using a best fit approach.

In this research, we introduce a novel functional stochastic differential equation framework to model the random motion of vortices in superfluids and superconductors, where the noise is influenced by the distances between vortices and varies over time. We apply this framework to a specific scenario: the interaction of three vortices in different two-dimensional superfluids and superconductors, and then extend it to a more general case with an arbitrary number of vortices. We also explore the numerical methods for the functional SDEs that arise in these scenarios.

The boson sampling model relies on the measurement of a single photon state interacting with a multi-mode interferometer, resulting in data that is typically analyzed using the Fock basis. However, this approach overlooks the full state of the photons, leading to questions about its potential for increased information. Our research involves a detailed study of two-photon states produced in boson sampling, using a quantum state transfer protocol to demonstrate that these states exhibit quantum properties like entanglement and non-locality, as measured by specific indicators. Our findings suggest that these states are genuinely entangled, and we propose a method to map their state space, enabling the development of more sophisticated sampling models.

In various life science studies, researchers need to analyze short, complex time series data that often include irrelevant information. This can be problematic when trying to identify meaningful patterns in such data. To address this challenge, we developed a new model that uses prior knowledge to guide the learning process. This model, called the guided autoregressive integrated moving average (GARIMA), is an extension of the autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) model. By incorporating prior information, GARIMA can learn more efficiently from smaller datasets, including those with irrelevant information. We tested GARIMA's performance using simulated data and found that it outperformed traditional ARIMA models. Additionally, we applied GARIMA to a real-world experiment where it accurately characterized the behavior of single molecules in a cellular environment.

Reinforcement learning in complex, dynamic environments with hidden factors is a major challenge in fields like AI and neurobiology. To address this issue, we focus on a simplified model where an agent interacts with its surroundings through a limited set of sensory inputs. From a neural network perspective, we examine how a recurrently connected architecture can be used to develop effective policies using sensory data and make informed predictions about the underlying hidden state. Our analysis reveals that a specific type of neural network, known as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMCP), is capable of achieving optimal policies and accurately estimating the likelihood of the agent's current situation. Additionally, we have found that POMCP-based neural networks can be designed to mimic the principles of Bayesian filtering, which is a widely recognized method for navigating uncertain environments.

Action detection, a task combining action classification and object classification, requires precise object context information to achieve high accuracy. However, current action detection models often overlook context objects, relying on frames or segments with annotated actions instead. This paper proposes a weakly-supervised action detection approach that identifies essential context objects for every action using association learning. We introduce a novel model that integrates action association and object association for context learning through graph convolutional networks. Our method leverages action-object pairs and object-object pairs to derive context objects without requiring bounding boxes. Experimental results on the JHMDB-21 and ActivityNet datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, yielding state-of-the-art performance on action detection benchmarks.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, held alongside ISBI 2021, brought together researchers to address the issue of detecting and removing image duplication, a crucial task in various fields including medicine, where it can indicate potential cases of image manipulation. A dataset comprising 100,000 medical images, used in testing the image duplication detection process, was compiled from abdominal CT scans. A total of 54 teams participated in the challenge, submitting 1,111 unique solutions, with the top 10 teams' results and findings described below.

This study investigates the asymptotic properties of boundary value problems for linear parabolic equations with small boundary perturbations, focusing on the behavior of solutions and their derivatives near the boundary. The analysis is conducted using a weighted Sobolev space framework, and we derive an asymptotic expansion for the boundary value problem, establish convergence theorems, and introduce a boundary operator that encodes the behavior of solutions. Our findings are applied to a metastability model involving a diffusion process in a domain with a small hole, and we demonstrate how the boundary value problem can be used to determine the transition time between metastable states. Additionally, we explore the asymptotic behavior of boundary value problems for a Dirichlet process with small boundary perturbations, and establish a convergence result in the format of a corrector theorem.

In this research, an investigation of the impact of strong magnetic fields on the properties of nuclear matter was carried out using the Lo\v{c}ov technique. Our findings indicate that the effect of the magnetic field on the equation of state at higher densities is minimal, but it has a more pronounced effect at lower densities. The research also shows that the magnetic field increases the binding energy and the pressure of nuclear matter at the saturation point, but it has no significant effect on the nuclear matter density at this point. The magnetic field was found to decrease the calculated neutron-to-proton ratio, but it did not affect the calculated caloric curve and the speed of sound in nuclear matter. The research also explored the effect of the magnetic field on the phase transition from nuclear to quark-gluon matter, and it was found that the magnetic field can cause a phase transition in neutron-rich matter when it is exposed to a sufficiently high intensity.

In recent years, Federated Learning (FL) has gained significant attention for enabling collaborative model training across multiple edge devices while maintaining their data privacy. Nonetheless, existing FL frameworks have not effectively addressed the issue of differential privacy to safeguard users' sensitive data. This paper proposes a novel approach called DP-REC, an innovative differential privacy technique for FL, which leverages the concept of record fragmentation to facilitate efficient and secure learning processes. By applying DP-REC to the Federated Recursive Averaging framework, we achieve substantial privacy guarantees for edge devices, while also achieving substantial communication efficiency improvements over conventional FL methods. Experimental results demonstrate that DP-REC yields a communication efficiency enhancement of up to 8 times and a privacy improvement of 4 orders of magnitude compared to the Federated Recursive Averaging framework.

The TPA complex is a nearby star-forming region visible in the NUV camera's wavelength range. Our observations revealed a large amount of diffuse FUV emission surrounding young stars in the TPA complex. The diffuse emission is not detected in X-ray images of the same area, suggesting that the diffuse FUV emission is primarily caused by photons from the Lyman series. The observed diffuse FUV emission is concentrated around young stars and is more intense near stars that emit more X-rays. The relationship between the diffuse FUV emission and X-ray emission is more significant in the TPA complex than in the nearby L43 star-forming region.
