This paper is a continuation of earlier research that developed innovative methods to control the conservation of mass and momentum in incompressible fluid flow. Building on those findings, we expand our approach to the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, where the flow density and velocity are interconnected through the continuity equation and Navier-Stokes equations. By establishing a new type of system with augmented controls, we demonstrate the conservation of a key integral related to mass and momentum, thus paving the way for the creation of control methods that preserve these physical principles.

This study evaluates the performance of several machine learning models, including Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, Support Vector Machine, and Neural Network, on a dataset of non-performing loans from a Greek bank. The models are trained on a dataset comprising 2,200 instances of borrowers with 11 predictive features, and their performance is assessed using 10-fold cross-validation. The results indicate that Random Forest and XGBoost achieve high accuracy, precision, and F1-score, while also identifying the most influential features for predicting non-performing loans.

This discussion expands upon the concept of chromatic symmetric functions of specific combinatorial structures known as Dyck trails. Utilizing q-rook theory in an innovative manner, we derive formulas for the CFGs of these trails in a parameterized form. Furthermore, we present novel CFGs for inverted Dyck trails of a particular type.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been the gold standard for image recognition tasks, but they have limitations in terms of efficiency and flexibility. To address these issues, a new type of neural network called Directional Convolutional Networks (DCNs) is proposed. DCNs utilize Directional Convolution (DirCon) layers that introduce directional bias into the convolution operation, resulting in a more efficient and flexible architecture. The DirCon layer's performance is comparable to standard convolutional layers, and it can be used in various configurations to achieve improved results. The DCN architecture is evaluated on image classification tasks, and it demonstrates superior performance and increased efficiency compared to traditional CNNs.

We establish a novel relative trace formula, which serves as a modified iteration of the classical relative trace formula by Arthur. By leveraging the geometric strategy pioneered by Beuzart-Plessis--Liu--Zhang--Zhu, we prove the relative trace formula's linear and curved versions are equivalent. Furthermore, we derive the curved linear periods from the geometric data, and our results have implications for the central class case, yielding insights into the geometry of Shimura varieties.

The light quark contribution to the top quark mass correction in the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ scheme can be estimated using the known light quark masses and a calculated parameter, denoted as $L_4^{ls}$. This parameter is determined through the standard perturbative QCD methods and depends on the masses of the light quarks. Since the light quark masses are not precisely known, we calculate the parameter $L_4^{ls}$ for different scenarios of the light quark masses, thereby enabling the computation of the light quark contribution to the top quark mass with varying degrees of uncertainty.

In 2007, Chvátal and Harary introduced the concept of edge-tinting for graphs, where each edge is assigned a unique color from the set of natural numbers. They posed a question regarding whether every graph with a certain level of regularity and a minimum degree of 3 could be edge-tinted in a sequential manner. This paper answers that query in the affirmative for graphs with specific properties and a subset of vertices meeting certain criteria.

We derive hypercontractive inequalities for functions within weighted Berman spaces, specifically tailored for the symmetric group S_n. Furthermore, analogous inequalities are also established for the type I Berberman spaces associated with GL(n, F_q), where F_q represents the finite field with q elements.

The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in an unprecedented number of infections and
deaths worldwide, underscoring the need for early and accurate detection of the
disease. Computed tomography scans, particularly high-dose scans that are
radiotoxic, have been widely employed to diagnose COVID-19. Low-dose CT scans,
being safer and more accessible, offer a promising alternative for detection.
However, low-quality images present a significant challenge for deep learning
algorithms. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel two-stage
time-distributed capsule network architecture that leverages both global and local
features to identify pneumonia caused by SARS-CoV-2. Our approach, which uses
ground truth data to inform the training process, achieves a high level of accuracy
in detecting COVID-19 from low-dose CT scans.

In recent years, particularly since the 2010s, there has been a significant surge in the number of artificial objects in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO), with this trend expected to continue as satellite constellations continue to expand. This increase in objects poses a significant risk to the safety of operational spacecraft, as well as their functionality, with potential malfunctions often being attributed to collisions with debris. To mitigate these risks, it is essential to optimize the spatial arrangement of operational spacecraft, thereby minimizing their likelihood of encountering hazardous objects. This study aims to develop a comprehensive framework for identifying suitable locations for operational spacecraft to occupy within LEO, with this space being defined as the area within which a spacecraft can safely operate without colliding with existing objects.

The creation of top-quality meshes for complex 3D designs is a crucial yet intricate process. Current mesh generation techniques often produce high-quality meshes, but they lack the advanced features needed to handle intricate engineering designs with complex topologies. In contrast, automated mesh generation tools typically require significant human input, including the adjustment of numerous parameters. To address this issue, researchers have developed a new method that leverages advanced mathematical programming to create high-order meshes with complex topologies. This approach uses a novel mesh configuration strategy, dividing the mesh into tetrahedrons and quadrilaterals, and employs integer linear programming to optimize mesh quality. In addition, the method's ability to handle curved surfaces and support multiple materials has been integrated. The results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in producing high-quality meshes with complex topologies, surpassing existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This research introduces a novel method for calculating the sample moments of the sample correlation in datasets. Building on a geometric framework, we develop an analytical expression for the probability distribution of the sample correlation in a k-dimensional space. By extending this approach to hyper-arrangements of n-dimensional space, we obtain a general formula for calculating the sample moments of the sample correlation. To demonstrate the practical application of this method, we apply it to compute the second sample moment of the sample correlation in 2-dimensional space. Furthermore, we use the derived formula to develop an efficient algorithm for calculating the sample correlation and associated statistical measures in large datasets.

We present a method for calculating the generalised $S$-matrix in the generalised Einstein gravity framework, which encompasses thin and thick branes, from fundamental strings to certain modified gravity theories. The key concept here is the generalised Pomarol framework, which involves a scalar mediator with a specific symmetry breaking pattern. By applying the generalised $S$-matrix to this scenario, we can derive a model-independent representation of the $S$-matrix that can be used to characterise scattering processes in a variety of gravity models. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to calculate the generalised $S$-matrix in the presence of a non-trivial background field, which is essential for understanding certain modified gravity theories.

We examine the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with weak solutions in a specific space. The goal is to achieve global uniform stabilization using a feedback control system. The evolution of the solution is governed by a nonlinear, low-regularity, and time-invariant force. The solution is initially bounded in a specific space and satisfies a specific inequality. The force is also assumed to have certain properties. The solution's trajectory is controlled by a finite-dimensional, localized feedback control system. The solution's stability is achieved through a specific, time-varying control function. The solution's regularity is improved using a specific inequality, and the solution is shown to be in a specific space. The solution's stability is achieved through a specific, time-varying control function, and the solution is shown to be in a specific space.

Language learning and research applications require comprehensive dictionaries to provide accurate word meanings and usage examples. Current online dictionaries, such as those from Cambridge and Oxford, are limited in their coverage and only accessible through a subscription or a paid download. To address this issue, we've developed the LitMind Lexicon, a free open-source dictionary that can be accessed online. The dictionary contains 1.7 million entries, including 200,000 definitions, 100,000 example sentences, and 50 million word counts from 5.5 billion tokens in the Gigaword Corpus. The example sentences in the dictionary are manually curated from the Corpus of Contemporary English to illustrate word usage. The LitMind Lexicon also includes a search function that allows users to look up words and their associated definitions, examples, and frequency information.

The increasing visibility of explainable AI has led to a growing demand for user-friendly models that provide transparent explanations. In the context of recommender systems, research has primarily focused on understanding why a particular item was suggested, rather than why certain items were omitted from the recommendation list. To address this gap, we introduce the Adherence-Aware Post-hoc Local Interpretable Model-based Aggregations (ALIMA) method, which enhances the LIME-RS model to improve the consistency of its explanations. By leveraging the strengths of both LIME-RS and other models, ALIMA aggregates and refines the feature importance scores to produce more accurate and consistent explanations. Experimental results demonstrate that ALIMA surpasses LIME-RS in adherence and consistency, while also rivaling state-of-the-art models in explanation quality.

Theoretical research has been conducted on the electronic characteristics of InAs quantum wells situated in close proximity to the surface within a 2DEG environment.  The 2DEG originates from the valence band maximum of GaAs, which is in close proximity to the InAs well.  The influence of surface states on the Fermi level position is investigated, and it is discovered that pinning of the Fermi level at the surface results in a 2DEG state that is separated from the conduction band minimum by an energy barrier.  The position of the 2DEG state relative to the Fermi level is found to be dependent on the InAs well thickness.  Theoretical calculations of the 2DEG and hole wave functions, as well as their respective energy levels, are presented.  The results demonstrate that InAs quantum wells with a well thickness of approximately one monolayer exhibit both 2DEG and hole confinement within the InAs well.  In contrast, InAs quantum wells with a well thickness exceeding one monolayer display 2DEG confinement within the InAs well while exhibiting delocalization of the hole wave function into the GaAs barrier.

In machine learning, a global model is often trained using data from multiple locations, which can help address issues related to overfitting and improving generalization. However, a different approach, known as local learning, trains separate models for each location, which can be beneficial when there's a significant difference in data quality or noise level across locations. While local learning is typically used for classification tasks, we explore its application in regression problems. We examine scenarios where local learning is more effective than traditional learning methods and develop a statistical framework to compare model performance. This framework is then applied to real-world datasets, which demonstrate the advantages of local learning in regression tasks.

Our previous work introduced an efficient kernel-based algorithm for computing the Sinkhorn matrix. This matrix serves as a key component in the Sinkhorn iteration used to solve the optimal transport problem. By leveraging kernel-based methods, we achieved a time complexity of O(n^2) per iteration. Building on this concept, we have developed an innovative approach to compute the Sinkhorn matrix, capitalizing on its triangular structure. This novel method allows us to compute each matrix column in linear time, thereby reducing the overall Sinkhorn iteration complexity to O(n) per iteration.

The AU Mic system, consisting of a nearby young star and two planets, offers a unique opportunity to study planetary atmospheres in their early stages of development. Observations by the AstroSat mission in the far-ultraviolet wavelength range reveal the star's behavior in its dormant and flaring states. Data from the star show signs of variability, with a decrease in its emission in the 125-145 nm wavelength range during a flare and a distinct increase in its emission in the 145-155 nm wavelength range in its dormant state. These changes are attributed to the presence of a hydrogen absorption edge and a possible emission line, respectively. These findings have implications for the atmospheres of the planets in the system, with possible effects on their ability to retain heat and support liquid or gaseous states.

We explore how a medium with resistance affects the movement of a charged particle under the influence of electromagnetic radiation. The impact of the medium's resistance causes the particle's motion to be slowed down, and this phenomenon is quantified through a drag coefficient that depends on the radiation intensity. By using a relativistic approach, we derive an equation for this drag coefficient in terms of the medium's properties and the radiation intensity, and this equation can be applied across various high-energy processes involving intense electromagnetic fields. The effects of the medium's resistance are particularly significant in processes involving high-energy particles and intense radiation, and this drag effect can potentially hinder the emission of particles from the vicinity of black holes and other regions with high radiation intensities.

The simplest yet most widely used classification method in machine learning is the nearest neighbor algorithm. Despite its straightforward concept, it presents several complex issues when applied to unbalanced datasets. This paper addresses these challenges by developing a novel nearest neighbor classification approach for unbalanced data. This method combines the nearest neighbor classifier with a weighted voting system among neighbors, where the weights are assigned according to the relative rarity of each class in the training set. To further enhance classification performance, the proposed method also utilizes a local reweighting technique, recalibrating the importance of each data point based on the number of misclassified neighbors. The proposed algorithm is supported by asymptotic theory and its validity is demonstrated through simulation studies and real-world applications.

Our research involves an extensive survey of ultra-bright quasars located at immense distances using the SkyMapper optical telescope. By analyzing a vast dataset of 13 million sources, we have identified 25 new quasars located at a vast distance, stretching from 6.2 to 7.5 billion light-years away. These discoveries significantly expand the known population of ultra-bright quasars in this distance range, allowing us to better understand their distribution. We have also developed a new model to describe how these extremely luminous objects are dispersed across space. By assuming that the known population of ultra-bright quasars is representative of the entire sample, we have determined that there are 0.015 +/- 0.005 quasars per cubic megaparsec that surpass a certain threshold of luminosity. This discovery is consistent with our understanding of how these objects evolve over time. Furthermore, we have calculated that the known population of ultra-bright quasars accounts for only 0.3 percent of the total number of quasars that exist but have not yet been detected.

The interaction between a quantum dot and a superconducting island in hybrid devices is a key component for creating and studying Majorana modes. However, the mechanisms underlying charge tunneling between these components are still unclear. Researchers have proposed various charge-tunneling mechanisms, but their experimental validation is needed. In this study, we employed a quantum dot-superconducting island hybrid device and developed a technique to detect charge tunneling through electrical sensing. By analyzing the device's conductance and using a non-linear response to a gate voltage, we identified single-electron and Cooper-pair tunneling as the primary mechanisms driving charge tunneling.

This study provides a mathematical framework for a specific type of shockwave that occurs in systems of equations, and investigates the stability of this shockwave under certain conditions. The research focuses on a particular class of systems known as hyperbolic, and demonstrates that a standard method for analyzing the stability of shockwaves is applicable to these systems. The findings of this study are significant because they offer a theoretical basis for understanding the behavior of shockwaves in various physical and engineering applications, and also shed light on the relationship between different types of shockwaves and waves in the context of these systems.

Creating a continuous and consistent view from a single image is a difficult task, especially when dealing with changing lighting conditions. Our new model, DiffDreamer, successfully generates novel views from a given image, along with their corresponding in-camera projections, by leveraging the capabilities of a conditional diffusion model in conjunction with a projection-based rendering technique. By integrating a projection module that utilizes the known camera parameters and 3D object data, we can accurately represent the observed image as a combination of the rendered view and lighting effects. Our approach allows for the separation of the input image into its intrinsic view and lighting components, which can then be used to generate new views under varying lighting conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that DiffDreamer outperforms existing models by producing more realistic and diverse views, and we also present a new benchmark for evaluating view generation performance.

A data-driven framework that uses machine learning has been developed to analyze and optimize complex systems. This approach, which relies solely on observed data, enables the prediction and optimization of system outcomes. By employing a two-step process, it's possible to first forecast the system's behavior under different conditions, and then identify the optimal settings that achieve specific goals. This framework has been successfully applied to a model of epidemic spread, where it's used to identify the optimal combination of control measures to minimize the impact of outbreaks.

The dynamics of a liquid layer on a fiber are studied using the axisymmetric approximation, and it's observed that as the liquid layer thins, instability on the fiber surface occurs earlier than expected within the conventional Rayleigh-Plateau (R-P) instability timescale. This accelerated instability is attributed to enhanced flow at the liquid-fiber interface, where the slip at the liquid-fiber interface amplifies the R-P instability growth rate. Consequently, the size of the liquid droplets formed from the liquid layer on fibers is found to decrease with increasing slip and decreased viscosity, and the droplet size is also found to decrease as the fiber diameter decreases.

We establish Lipschitz stability within solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation, which exhibit geometric significance as they govern the dynamics of a curve's rotation minimization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the left Lipschitz condition applies to solutions when considering the curve's arc length parameterization.

A novel robotic ultrasound system, capable of automatically positioning and guiding an ultrasound probe to measure spinal curvature, has been developed. To evaluate its performance, a study compared robotic and manual scanning techniques for assessing scoliosis using ultrasound. Scoliosis assessments were conducted on 30 individuals with known spinal curvature using both robotic and manual scanning methods, and measurements from both procedures were recorded and analyzed. Results showed that robotic scanning produced reliable and accurate measurements comparable to those obtained through manual scanning, with a high degree of consistency between the two methods. Furthermore, the study found a strong correlation between scoliosis assessments using both robotic and manual scanning, with a correlation coefficient of 0.98. These findings suggest that robotic scanning is a viable and reliable alternative to manual scanning for scoliosis assessment, with potential applications expanding to other spinal conditions.

This study introduces a novel duration modeling approach for synthesizing speech, where a non-parametric statistical method is used to create synthetic data by mediating the gap between actual and desired duration values. Unlike traditional approaches, this method does not rely on specific probability distributions being applicable to a given dataset. As a result, it can effectively handle datasets with complex patterns. A comparison of this method with existing approaches, including a Gaussian mixture model, revealed that it yields superior synthetic data. A subjective listening test also confirmed that the quality of synthesized speech using this method is comparable to that using a Gaussian mixture model.

Hate speech on social media is a significant problem, spreading negativity and
hatred among people. Researchers have been working to address this issue through
automatic hate speech detection, but the task is complex due to the use of
offensive language and hate symbols. Prior studies have employed machine learning
and deep learning methods, but a new approach using feature selection techniques
could be effective. This paper proposes a model that combines feature selection
with support vector classification to identify hate speech. The proposed method
uses a combination of syntactic, semantic, and syntactic & semantic features to
classify posts as hate speech. Experiment results on two datasets demonstrate
that the proposed method performs better than existing approaches.

Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) networks, which process multiple inputs and outputs, have seen significant success in various computer vision tasks. However, their full potential in video understanding has not been fully realized. This is largely due to the way MIMO modules share features across different inputs, which is not tailored to the unique characteristics of video data. In our research, we investigate the feature sharing mechanism within MIMO networks and demonstrate its impact on the performance of video understanding models. Based on our findings, we develop a new feature sharing strategy that adapts to the spatial and temporal properties of video data, which leads to improved performance when applied to MIMO networks.

This study provides a comprehensive review of the most prominent datasets used
in the analysis of historical manuscript images. These datasets are specifically
designed for tasks like document reconstruction, text extraction, and transcription,
and are distinguished by their unique characteristics, which pose significant
challenges in the form of degradation, distortion, and formatting variations. To
better understand the evolution of this field, the study also examines the
techniques employed by previous researchers to create and label these datasets.
Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of these datasets in facilitating
research and development in the field and outlines potential future directions
for creating new, more comprehensive datasets that can aid in the advancement of
methods for historical manuscript analysis.

This research proposes a novel flatness-based approach to regulate robot joint movements using supplementary position sensors. Flatness-based control is a promising method for trajectory planning, yet it typically necessitates the use of additional measurement tools to determine derivative values. To overcome this limitation, a regulation strategy is presented that requires only one additional position sensor per actuated joint, allowing for the computation of flatness-based derivative values without the need for state observers. The proposed approach is evaluated through both simulation and practical experiments using an ABB IRB 6600 robot.

This study examines the impact of modifiable lifestyle factors on future heart disease in patients who have already experienced a heart attack. To achieve this, researchers analyzed data from a large cohort of 7,536 Australian heart attack survivors, focusing on the effects of physical activity, smoking, and a healthy diet on subsequent cardiovascular events. A novel approach, Multiple State Examination, was employed to investigate how combinations of these lifestyle factors influence individuals. Results indicate that a healthy diet has the most significant influence on future heart disease, with smoking being the next most critical factor. Physical inactivity also increases the risk, although this effect is less pronounced than that of smoking. Furthermore, the study found that individuals who experience multiple risk factors face a higher risk of additional heart disease, with a 2.5-fold increased risk for those with three risk factors compared to those with none.

A novel integration scheme has been developed for modeling molecular flow interacting with a solid surface. This method combines a multi-point approach to efficiently handle the large pressure gradients at the solid-liquid interface. Additionally, an adaptive grid refinement technique is employed to minimize computational costs. The integration scheme is based on a multi-step method that uses a combination of first-order and second-order spatial approximations, as well as first-order and second-order temporal predictions. The method's accuracy is evaluated using various numerical tests, including a test of stability, a test of spatial convergence, and a test of temporal convergence. The results show that the method achieves the desired level of accuracy in each test.

The metric dimension problem, which involves determining the minimum number of markers required to uniquely locate all vertices in a graph, has been explored through parameterized complexity theory. Researchers have established upper bounds for solving this problem with various constraints, including feedback vertex number and other structural parameters. Specifically, they have shown that the problem can be solved in O*(1) time for each value of the chosen parameter in a single parameter, as well as in O*(1) time for each value of two chosen parameters. These results were obtained by analyzing upper bounds for the localized feedback vertex number, which can be solved in single-exponential time, and the induced neighborhood cover parameter, which has a single-exponential search time.

Directed spaces, which have a separate concept of direction that can differ from the original metric, are explored in this study. The interplay between upper directed metric spaces and the power framework is examined, which involves transforming a directed metric into an upper directed metric using a continuous function. The study establishes the power frameworks of these spaces, which are shown to be the largest class where the power framework operation is well-defined. The work also considers the subframeworks of directed spaces, which are the smallest class where the power framework operation is well-defined. The study compares and contrasts the power frameworks with subframeworks in various settings, including the case of directed p-metric spaces.

Future climate projections suggest that Earth may experience a 'hothouse' state with significantly higher temperatures and more intense precipitation. This study uses cloud-resolving simulations to examine precipitation patterns in a 'hothouse' climate, focusing on the characteristics of extreme downpours that are not accurately simulated by coarser resolution models. By analyzing precipitation statistics from 1000 model runs with a 10-meter grid resolution, researchers found that approximately 1% of these simulations exhibited extreme downpours, characterized by precipitation exceeding 1 cm/min. These events were largely confined to tropical regions and were associated with deep convection and heavy precipitation. In contrast, downpours in mid-latitude regions were often linked to convection and were less intense. These findings have significant implications for flood risk assessment and management, as they suggest that precipitation patterns in a 'hothouse' climate may be more unpredictable and prone to extreme variability.

In this study, we investigate the construction of twistor operators for Yang-Mills theory and its self-dual counterpart in four-dimensional spacetime, as well as the higher-spin generalizations of these theories. We demonstrate that twistor operators exist for Yang-Mills theory when coupled with spinor chiralities, but not in a supersymmetric framework. However, for self-dual Yang-Mills theory, twistor operators can be constructed without spinor chiralities. We then explore the higher-spin extensions of these theories, revealing that twistor operators can be constructed for these theories as well, but only when the spinor chiralities are involved.

Deep learning's success in medical image classification is hindered by noisy labels, which can be corrected through label refinement. However, existing methods rely on additional clean labels, which are scarce in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a noise detection mechanism that utilizes Bayesian statistics to identify incorrect labels. By eliminating noise from the training dataset, our approach achieves noise-free supervision and improves model performance. Experimental results on three medical datasets confirm that our method effectively mitigates label noise and yields better classification outcomes.

This study examines the norm of an interpolation projector in the context of a Hilbert space with an infinite sequence of orthonormal basis. The upper bounds for the norm are established under specific conditions on the sequence elements. The derived bounds are relevant to the analysis of convergence rates in best approximation problems and have practical implications in coding theory, with particular references to Gelfand-Shilov spaces.

A random walk's (RW) transition probability matrix (TPM) governs the probabilities of a particle transitioning between graph vertices. The RW's stationary probability distribution, which indicates equilibrium states, relies on the TPM's eigenvalues and eigenvectors. However, calculating these values becomes increasingly difficult as graph size increases, making associated algorithms computationally challenging. To address this issue, a characteristic polynomial has been derived for the TPM, which can be used to determine the eigenvalues of the TPM. This development enables the application of the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, allowing users to calculate the associated eigenvalues without directly computing or storing the TPM. The paper also discusses how this finding can be utilized to determine the stationary distribution of the RW and its associated eigenvectors.

In this work, we develop a method for incorporating functions with time limitations into the HOL proof assistant, allowing for the representation of such functions as individual axioms within a theorem library. Furthermore, we propose a technique for incrementally adding timed definitions to a theorem library, accompanied by an examination of the implications for automated reasoning tools. A case study involving the development of a timed function for computing the Euclidean division is presented to illustrate the concept in action.

A novel, coherent structure-based model for predicting instantaneous wall-pressure and wall-shear-stress in wall-bounded turbulent flows has been developed. This model leverages a detailed understanding of the organized motion within wall turbulence, utilizing a specific coherent structure to simulate wall-turbulence. By incorporating a model for random, incoherent motions on top of the coherent structure model, a comprehensive model for predicting instantaneous wall-turbulence has been achieved. The incoherent motion model is based on a traditional eddy-viscosity approach, with its effects combined with the coherent structure model. The resulting model has been successfully validated against a wide range of experimental data from various wall-bounded turbulent flows, with the model's predictions showing excellent agreement across different geometries and Reynolds numbers.

We introduce a modified Skyrme model incorporating a Born-Infeld term with a specific symmetry, which allows for the derivation of a simplified equation in a simple gauge. By exploiting this equation, we demonstrate the existence of self-dual solitons in the model.

In three-dimensional Weyl semimetals, a time-reversal-breaking chemical potential results in a unique phase at finite magnetic field strength, characterized by the presence of a single Chern number. We investigate the phase diagram of this phase using a tight-binding model on a hypercubic lattice, incorporating a random potential and a magnetic field. Our findings reveal that the phase diagram transitions from a smooth curve at low magnetic field strength to a complex pattern of phase boundaries at higher field strength, marked by the appearance of multiple phase boundaries and isolated regions of distinct topology.

The integration of dielectric and plasmonic materials in nanoantennas has been a highly effective approach for manipulating light at the nanoscale. In this study, we propose a novel design for a hybrid nanoantenna consisting of a central dielectric core surrounded by plasmonic nanorods, which exhibits unique optical properties. The design allows for the creation of a unidirectional photon source with adjustable emission patterns and can be used to produce entangled photons through spontaneous parametric down conversion. The design's performance is influenced by the optical properties of the material and the geometry of the nanoantenna, with the potential to achieve high entanglement rates.

A 2018 theory, known as anomalous screening, posits that particles in a granular medium can generate an unusual electric potential at short intervals, contrary to traditional expectations. Researchers have now experimentally and computationally verified this concept in a granular column subjected to a vibration. By analyzing the potential generated at different depths, they found that the anomalous screening effect is accurately represented by a specific mathematical equation that describes the potential with two distinct parameters - the screening length and a coupling constant. Furthermore, numerical simulations using the discrete element method confirmed the theory's applicability in granular systems.

In this research, we investigate the influence of hexagonal boron nitride on silicene using the density functional theory method. Our study involves comparing the electronic properties of silicene on a boron nitride substrate with those of bulk silicon and silicene on a gold surface. Additionally, we examine the impact of manganese decoration on the properties of single and double-layer silicene on boron nitride. Our findings suggest that manganese decoration results in a half-metallic state in both single and double-layer silicene, with a magnetic moment of 3.0 mu_B per manganese atom.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, is a pivotal subject in astrophysics due to its proximity to the supermassive black hole at its center. Researchers have extensively analyzed the remnant's properties, but the origin of the supernova that created the remnant and the timing of its explosion remain unclear. A new study aims to shed light on these questions by modeling the remnant's expansion and examining the effects of the supermassive black hole's gravity on its evolution. By comparing the model's predictions to observational data, the researchers found that a supernova that occurred approximately 10-20 million years ago, with an initial explosion energy of around 10^51 erg, is consistent with observations of the remnant's size, expansion velocity, and X-ray emission. However, the model's predictions for the remnant's central pressure and kinetic energy are higher than those observed, suggesting that the supernova likely occurred in a dense star cluster rather than a typical open cluster.

Overampling, a technique used in machine learning, involves creating additional training examples to enhance the training process. This can be done by either selecting existing data or generating new examples synthetically. This study focuses on the latter approach, comparing three synthetic oversampling methods for improving multi-class text classification. These methods incorporate natural language models to produce text based on class labels, use word embeddings to create text based on instances, and combine these approaches. The results indicate that a hybrid method which combines these techniques performs best overall, with significant improvements in performance observed for the word-embedding based method when data is scarce.

This study examines the relationship between local news coverage, COVID-19 cases and deaths, and audience characteristics in the United States. It first develops an index of local news coverage based on a comprehensive dataset of articles from major newspapers. Next, it uses a spatial analysis to test the correlation between this coverage and COVID-19 cases and deaths across 210 metropolitan areas. The findings reveal a significant negative correlation between local news coverage and COVID-19 cases and deaths. The research also reveals that areas with higher local news coverage tend to have lower case and death rates, after controlling for demographic factors. Furthermore, the study shows that local news coverage is influenced by audience characteristics, such as age, education, and political leaning. The results suggest that local news can play a crucial role in mitigating the spread of COVID-19.

The fast multipole method has been widely used for accelerating the computations of n-body problems and their extensions in various fields. Although it effectively reduces the computational complexity, the original implementation did not account for the conservation of angular momentum in collisionless systems. As a result, inaccurately modeled interactions in distant regions can lead to spurious angular momentum transfer between particles, causing artificial orbital decay and alignment. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel formulation of the fast multipole method that ensures the preservation of angular momentum in three-body interactions. Our approach involves modifying the monopole term to account for the conservation of angular momentum, and we have conducted thorough analyses to validate its accuracy and efficiency. Our results demonstrate that the revised fast multipole method accurately conserves angular momentum while maintaining the same level of computational performance as the standard implementation.

The aim of this research is to investigate the phenomenon where polarization is transferred from the initial to the final proton in the elastic scattering process $e\vec{p} \to e\vec{p}$. The study reveals that, at an electron-proton center-of-mass scattering angle of 45 degrees, polarization transfer occurs efficiently at low and intermediate kinematics but diminishes at higher scattering angles. However, despite the presence of a virtual photon exchange, polarization transfer remains substantial even at large scattering angles. The research also indicates that, at a specific Q^2 value, the polarization transfer to the proton is independent of the electron's beam polarization, suggesting that measurements of this effect are best conducted using an unpolarized electron beam.

In the context of online learning, we investigate the challenge of reducing sample complexity when learning from multiple parametric experts, each with its own cost function. We focus on the particular case of Gaussian processes, which often serve as effective models for experts in this setting. To this end, we introduce a data augmentation method that significantly decreases the required number of samples to achieve optimal regret bounds. Building on this approach, we further develop a universal learning algorithm capable of performing well when given experts with more general cost functions.

A comprehensive study of the production of two Higgs bosons in conjunction with an electroweak boson has been conducted, utilizing 36.1 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV, collected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC in 2015-2016. The analysis targeted the pairs of Higgs bosons paired with W and Z bosons, specifically the Hq¯q, HW, and ZZ channels. By examining these channels, the study has set limits on the Higgs boson pair production cross-section and has made the first direct observation of the ZZ production with a 13 TeV Z boson at 5.8σ statistical significance. The observed limits on the Higgs boson pair production cross-section have been found to be at 0.37 pb (0.27 pb) at the 95% confidence level, assuming production in association with a W (Z) boson. The study has also set the most stringent constraints on the Higgs boson self-coupling, specifically a product of two Higgs boson self-coupling and a Higgs boson coupling to a vector boson, at 0.10 pb (0.19 pb) at the 95% confidence level. The study has also set the most stringent constraints on the Higgs boson pair production cross-section, specifically a product of two Higgs boson self-coupling and a Higgs boson

We've developed a unique laser system that utilizes a controlled digital signal to modulate an optical cavity, using a highly stable laser beam to produce a series of precisely defined optical pulses. By employing an optimized cavity layout and a specific digital driver, the laser beam can be modulated at extremely high speeds, allowing it to maintain coherence and produce a broad spectrum of frequencies. This innovative approach has made it possible to achieve a level of stability in the laser beam that is limited only by the speed of light, a significant improvement over previous technologies.

We establish a connection between extremely rare K3 surfaces, their 2-torsion and Siegel disks. Specifically, we demonstrate that for K3 surfaces with 16 or fewer rational curves, their 2-torsion in the Mordell-Weil group can be calculated using the K3 surface's period matrix, thereby offering an alternative method to existing approaches. Additionally, our work includes a case study involving K3 surfaces from the period matrix collection of Borel et al, yielding new insights into 2-torsion and Siegel disks for these K3 surfaces.

In the context of the lightest supersymmetric particle being the dominant component of dark matter, we examine the potential for neutralino decay into the chargino and neutrino, and calculate the resulting gamma ray emission spectra within the framework of the minimal supersymmetric standard model, incorporating two distinct scenarios of soft supersymmetry breaking: the mSUGRA model and the gaugino-hybrid model.

We establish an efficient algorithm that can efficiently approximate the genus of a given dense graph, with the desired level of accuracy, in polynomial time. Specifically, for any graph G with m edges and a target approximation factor better than epsilon > 0, the algorithm runs in O(m^(1.5 + 2/epsilon^2)) time. This solution builds upon a previous method by Leake and Wollmer (2019), with an improved dependency on epsilon. We also provide a modified version of the algorithm that can handle graphs with any degree distribution, in O(m^(1+ 2/epsilon^2)) time.

This paper presents a distributed stochastic Newton method for solving large-scale networked convex optimization problems. The proposed algorithm, STAN, combines the benefits of stochastic optimization and distributed Newton methods. At each iteration, a subset of nodes is randomly selected and updated using an inexact Newton-Raphson method via the average of locally computed gradients and hessian matrices. Theoretical convergence bounds for STAN are established, demonstrating a convergence rate of O(1/k) with a constant dependent on the condition number. The method's performance is evaluated through simulations on a network planning application.

This study delves into the detection of hate speech in two prominent South Asian languages, Hindi, and Bengali, highlighting the need for hate speech detection in online settings, particularly in countries like India where it has a significant impact on social cohesion. The research focuses on developing a universal model for both languages, employing transfer learning with a neural network architecture. The analysis utilizes a publicly accessible dataset to evaluate the effectiveness of different machine learning models, including traditional and deep learning approaches, on hate speech detection and classification tasks. The findings demonstrate that a neural network-based model leveraging word2vec and glove embeddings, trained on English and the two South Asian languages, performs exceptionally well across all three tasks, achieving an accuracy of 0.93 for multi-class classification and 0.90 for binary classification, with a precision of 0.93 for positive micro precision and 0.90 for recall.

In the context of high-energy neutrino detectors, particularly those utilizing large-volume low-pressure gas time projection chambers, accurately detecting recoil charges is crucial for identifying neutrino interactions. This process is complicated by the presence of ionization signals from the primary interaction and the more intense ionization signals from the incoming neutrino, which can obscure the recoil charges. To address this challenge, researchers have developed a set of observables designed to isolate the recoil charges by leveraging differences in their characteristics. These observables include the timing of the signals, their drift time-based positions, their lifetimes, and their amplitudes. By utilizing simulated data from the ProtoCUTE TPC, a detector under construction for the P280 experiment, researchers have demonstrated the effectiveness of these observables in isolating the recoil charges, with the amplitudes being the most decisive factor.

In the era of autonomous driving, AI systems are being trained to predict human behavior to improve safety and efficiency. However, these models often struggle to accurately predict actions in real-world commercial driving scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose a multi-faceted approach that combines machine learning with expert human input to better understand decision-making processes in complex driving situations. By integrating AI-driven predictions with expert feedback, we can refine and improve the accuracy of behavioral forecasting. Our approach also allows for the assessment of fairness in AI-driven predictions, enabling more precise and equitable risk assessments for commercial drivers.

The 2022 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision for Cultural Heritage featured an out-of-category competition that drew significant interest, with 24 teams participating out of 130 total entries across all competitions. This report outlines the competition's details and presents the findings of the top three winning teams in the out-of-category category.

We examine the geodesic paths within the manifold of a Gaussian random field (GRF). A GRF is a random function on a space that is both smooth and topologically connected. A geodesic path is a path that is optimal for predicting the GRF's likelihood given observations along the path. We demonstrate that geodesic paths are analytically tractable for GRFs with a specific covariance function, and provide a computationally efficient method for determining them in other cases through variational approximation. We also show that these paths are invariant to the scale of the observations and can be used to develop a hierarchical model.

This animated movie showcases the algorithm presented in the accompanying article. 
The algorithm's central idea is that the length of a knot or link segment oscillates between its actual value and the opposite value under a specific transformation, and this oscillation repeats at a specific interval. 
By monitoring these oscillations over time, we can calculate knot and link fusion lengths in an interactive 3D environment. 
The movie demonstrates this method for various knots and links, with a focus on minimal knot fusion bases, up to a certain level of complexity in the knot table.

We define a modulus $m$ as a product of two positive integers $a$ and $b$, with $a < b$. For a Siegel modular form $F$ of weight $k$, the L-function $L(s,F)$ has a known analytic continuation to the real line and a pole at $s=\frac{k+1}{2}$ with a specific order. The order of the pole is either infinite and bounded or zero. We call the former case a distinct L-function and the latter a distinct L-value. We investigate the boundedness of the denominators of distinct L-values, specifically for Maass forms of weight k for the symplectic group Sp(n), which have a known analytic continuation to the real line and a simple pole at s=(k+1)/2.

This research investigates the transport characteristics of armchair graphene nanoribbons with specific edge modifications to demonstrate spin-dependent behavior. Utilizing the nonequilibrium Green's functions method in combination with the density functional theory formalism, our study examines the influence of diverse atomic configurations on charge and spin transport. We found that spin current is highly susceptible to variations in atomic alignment, particularly when encountering head-to-head or tail-to-tail ferromagnetic barriers. In contrast, charge current is relatively less sensitive to these changes. Notably, our results show that spin current can be effectively controlled through the use of antiferromagnetic semiconducting barriers, which could have significant implications for the development of spintronics technology.

We establish Korovkin-type theorems for weakly nonlinear, monotone operators acting on C[0,1], and for linear operators on C[0,1]. Furthermore, these results are extended to multivariate operator theorems. In addition, we prove a nonlinear Korovkin theorem for operators acting on A[0,1].

A graph is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length. Research has focused on finding the tight bounds between a graph's independence number and its pancyclic properties. Specifically, for a given n, the task is to determine the smallest possible pancyclic graph, g(n), such that a given upper bound applies. Researchers, including Geller and Stemple in 1974, initially found g(n) with an upper bound of 2n/3. Later, Erdos and Gallai in 1961 discovered a graph with an upper bound of n/2, but it lacks pancyclic properties. In 1972, Erdos and Hajnal proposed the conjecture that every graph with n vertices contains either a complete subgraph of size n/2 or a complete bipartite subgraph of size n/4. In 1981, this conjecture was proven for bipartite graphs by Hal{\l}usz, in 1983 it was proven for all graphs by Bollobas and Thomason, and in 1990 it was proven for bipartite graphs with specific conditions by Kostochka. In 1990, it was proven that g(n) with an upper bound of n/2 is not possible in all cases.
